<reason>Both sides agreed by the end that the debate turns on what happens when age verification fails. B built a consistent asymmetry from the opening onward: under binding minor design law, protective defaults apply to unverified accounts so a lying fourteen-year-old lands on a safe product, whereas under a ban she lands on the full adult product because the law forbids a child account from existing. A's best attempts to break this—(1) design law also needs verification, (2) safe defaults don't stop adult DMs, (3) platforms will quietly degrade design rules—were each answered: B showed verification can be opt-in rather than compulsory using the very app-store mechanism A endorsed, pointed back to private-by-default contact rules already in [B1.2], and pressed the "pick one" symmetry that if fines can make platforms verify invisible birthdays they can make them ship visible feed changes. A never resolved that symmetry and, by narrowing the ban to "algorithmic accounts" while leaving messaging open, handed B the point that sextortion lives in the exact spaces A exempted. A was rhetorically crisp ("it's Tuesday") and correct that design law needs enforcement too, but B's closing made the choice concrete and easy to decide. Both sides suffered a clipped turn.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.1]–[B2.5]) inverted A's "one number is verifiable" framing—age is the one invisible variable, design rules are visible on the product surface—and paired it with the "every failure in my world is harmless, every failure in yours is total" asymmetry. B then sustained it in Rebuttal 2 by answering A's DM-grooming pressure question with the private-by-default contact rules already on the table, leaving A's closing with only the already-rebutted "casinos degrade rules" line.</best_rebuttal>
